name: XML
license: Open standard, free to implement (W3C Recommendation)
summary: The W3C’s markup language for trees of tagged text, still behind Office documents, SVG, feeds, SOAP and the S3 API.
intro: An XML document is a tree of elements. Each element has a start and end tag (`<order id="42">…</order>`, or `<empty/>`), and may hold attributes, text, other elements, comments (`<!-- -->`) and CDATA sections. A document must be well-formed: one root element, properly nested tags, quoted attribute values. When a parser finds a well-formedness error, the spec says it must stop passing data to the application. Everything is text: XML itself has no numbers or dates, and types come from a schema. An optional document type declaration (DTD) describes the allowed structure and defines entities, named pieces of replacement text, including external entities that point at a file or URL. Namespaces qualify element names with a URI, so vocabularies such as SVG can be mixed into other documents without name clashes.

The core spec is a W3C Recommendation, XML 1.0, now in its Fifth Edition (November 2008), and free to implement. Around it sit W3C XML Schema (XSD 1.1, 2012) for structure and data types, RELAX NG (ISO/IEC 19757-2) as a simpler schema language, and XPath 3.1 (2017) for selecting nodes. XML still defines Office Open XML documents (ECMA-376), SVG, RSS and Atom feeds and SOAP messages. Amazon S3’s REST API answers in XML, and Azure Blob Storage’s List Blobs returns XML unless a client asks for its newer Apache Arrow format.
strengths: Mature standards for validation (DTD, XSD, RELAX NG) and querying (XPath), so documents can be checked strictly
Mixed content (text with markup inside it) suits documents such as Office files and SVG
Namespaces let one document combine vocabularies from different owners without clashing names
Strict well-formedness: a broken document is rejected instead of being guessed at
limits: Verbose by design: the spec says terseness “is of minimal importance”, and every end tag repeats its name
No data types without a schema; every value arrives as text and the application converts it

Unsafe parser defaults: resolving DTDs and external entities opens the door to XXE (reading local files, server-side request forgery) and “billion laughs” entity-expansion attacks; OWASP’s advice is to disable DTDs entirely
Namespaces trip up code: S3 puts every element of its responses in a default namespace, so unqualified lookups find nothing

story: The Web of the mid-1990s served HTML, one fixed set of tags. SGML, the general markup standard, let anyone define their own tags, but its documents couldn’t be served on the Web the same way. In 1996 the W3C formed a working group, at first called the SGML Editorial Review Board and chaired by Jon Bosak of Sun Microsystems, to let “generic SGML” be served, received and processed on the Web the way HTML was. Its answer was a subset of SGML small enough to be described completely in one spec. Edited by Tim Bray, Jean Paoli and C. M. Sperberg-McQueen, XML 1.0 became a W3C Recommendation on 10 February 1998.

A family of standards grew around it: Namespaces in 1999, W3C XML Schema in 2001, and formats built on XML such as SOAP, RSS, Atom (2005) and Office Open XML (2006). In December 2006, Douglas Crockford pitched JSON to the XML 2006 conference as “the fat-free alternative to XML” for data exchange in browsers. The Fifth Edition of XML 1.0, published in November 2008, is still the current text.

choices.why: Compatibility with SGML was a design goal, so SGML tools could still process XML documents, while another goal kept XML easy to write programs for.

The goals asked for programs that are easy to write and for optional features to be kept to “the absolute minimum, ideally zero”. A processor that hits a well-formedness error must stop normal processing, so parsers don’t each invent their own recovery.
An explicit design goal. Clarity and easy processing beat compactness, which is why every end tag repeats its element’s name.

choices.choice: Namespaces as URIs, added a year later
choices.why: Mixing vocabularies needed globally unique names. The 1999 Namespaces spec qualified names with URIs, often written as web addresses, without changing XML 1.0 itself.
